extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students/practitioners of public relations, media studies, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards and tactics for designing and evaluating public-relations/press‑release style campaigns (techniques Bernays used or described). Covers tactics, ethical considerations, and procedural approaches illustrated by historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mass/crowd psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: View the masses as irrational and subject to herd instinct and design persuasion accordingly (page describes 'the masses as irrational and subject to herd instinct').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ insights from crowd psychology and psychoanalysis to shape messaging that leverages herd behaviors and automatic responses. Example: Bernays's general claim that 'touch a nerve at a sensitive spot and you get an automatic response from certain specific members of the organism.' Anti‑pattern: assuming individuals are fully rational and ignoring group-level triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering of consent / scientific opinion‑molding
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat public persuasion as a 'scientific technique of opinion‑molding' or 'engineering of consent' using social science methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns based on social-science research (surveys, experiments, social indicators) to predictably shape public attitudes. Bernays framed PR as a 'science' to manage information in ways most advantageous to an organization. Scoring note: stronger campaigns show empirical grounding and systematic design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of third parties / third‑party endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Covert or overt use of third parties who appear independent to diffuse messages ('the covert use of third parties was morally legitimate because those parties were morally autonomous actors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influence or enlist leaders, experts, social figures, or other organizations so they carry the message to their constituencies (e.g., physicians endorsing a heavier breakfast). Anti‑pattern: overreliance on direct advertising rather than third‑party signals when credibility is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal client identity / make publicity appear independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the counsel/client role hidden so publicity 'should appear as news with no division of the publicity' and not look like paid promotion (Bernays instructed staff never to mention his name in some campaigns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure releases, events, and placements so the source appears organic or independent (use anonymous reports, third-party spokespeople, or front organizations). Ethical caveat: concealment raises transparency and democratic-legitimacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage pseudo‑events and spectacles to generate news
rubrics_metrics.description: Create staged events (pancake breakfasts, themed balls, public marches) designed primarily to attract media coverage rather than represent spontaneous happenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan eye-catching, newsworthy actions timed and framed to maximize press attention (examples: Coolidge 'pancake breakfast', the Green Ball, Torches of Freedom parade). Measurement: media pickup and the framing of coverage are the intended outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist celebrities and notable cultural figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use performers, society leaders, and celebrities to give a campaign cultural visibility and perceived prestige (examples: Enrico Caruso, Flore Revalles, society women at the Green Ball).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select endorsers whose public image aligns with the campaign frame. Avoid obvious paid spokespeople if the goal is to create a sense of spontaneous endorsement; consider credibility and demographic fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experts and purported scientific authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicit and publish expert endorsements or research findings to lend legitimacy to claims (e.g., surveying physicians to back a 'bigger breakfast' claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission or publicize expert statements, letter campaigns, or surveys and seed them into media channels. Anti‑pattern: manufacturing dubious 'research' without transparency; risk of reputational harm if discredited later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link product/client interests to cultural or public values
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame a product or policy as aligned with broader cultural values or the public interest (e.g., bacon & eggs as 'all‑American breakfast'; bananas linked to health and American interests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create narratives that connect client goals to national identity, health, morality, or other widely held values so adoption appears normative. Success metric: uptake of the frame in media and public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messages to specific demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt messaging for different audience segments and demographics (example: advising a candidate to emphasize different issues to Irish, Italian, and Jewish voters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map audiences and vary framing, spokespeople, and channels by group. Evaluation: resonance and persuasion within targeted segments rather than one-size-fits-all messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute materials to 'opinion molders' and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Send reports, newsletters, and briefing materials to journalists, members of Congress, academics, and other influencers to shape elite discourse (e.g., Guatemala Newsletter distributed to 250 journalists; Report on Guatemala sent to Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and directly supply content to intermediaries who shape mainstream reporting and policy debate. Track placements, citations, and institutional uptake as success indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use media tours and sponsored journalist visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange trips or tours for journalists to shape their reporting and create sympathetic coverage (Bernays brought journalists on multiple Guatemala tours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate experiences and sources during sponsored visits to steer narrative and imagery. Ethical note: disclose sponsorship where appropriate; undisclosed trips may be criticized as manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and operate front groups or pseudo‑independent bureaus
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish organizations presented as independent (e.g., Middle America Information Bureau) to supply favorable information to press and academics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use front groups to reframe issues and produce materials that appear non-commercial or civic. Anti‑pattern: detection of the front group's true sponsor can nullify credibility and cause backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit stereotypes and preconceptions in framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharpen and use existing stereotypes or 'rubber stamp' preconceived ideas so audiences more readily accept new messaging (Bernays expands on Lippmann's concept of 'stereotype').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build on, rather than try to overturn, existing beliefs—reframe them into a desired picture. Measurement: how readily audiences accept the adjusted stereotype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid placements and covertly compensated promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay or otherwise compensate notable people to act as if independently endorsing a product or behavior (the article notes 'various notable people received payments to promote smoking publicly as if on their own initiative').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for influencer or surrogate compensation when covert endorsement is judged necessary, but weigh legal/ethical disclosure requirements and reputational risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization, planning, and professionalization of PR work
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate for coordinated, centralized planning, formal training, and institutionalization of public relations practice (Bernays pushed for licensing and university training of PR counselors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use organized, top-down campaign planning and professional standards to execute large-scale persuasion efforts. Evaluation criteria include coherence across channels, institutional coordination, and professional ethics governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present persuasion as news / avoid 'division of the publicity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft releases and actions so they read and are treated as news rather than as labeled advertising; Bernays emphasized 'it should appear as news with no division of the publicity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write factual-seeming releases, stage quotable moments, and embed claims in third-party reporting to maximize news value. Anti‑pattern: obvious advertorials that editors treat as paid content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply wartime 'psychological warfare' techniques to peacetime campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer techniques developed for wartime psychological operations (CPI experience) to commercial and political persuasion in peacetime—'what could be done for a nation at war could be done... in peacetime pursuits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage coordinated messaging, targeted propaganda-style playbooks, and international information efforts when appropriate. Ethical and legal considerations increase when techniques mirror wartime operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical transparency and democratic impact as evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess campaigns for their ethical implications: potential manipulation, undermining of individual autonomy, erosion of democratic engagement, and similarity to authoritarian propaganda (page documents criticisms and comparisons to Nazi propaganda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh persuasive effectiveness against transparency, public trust, and democratic norms. Use disclosure, accountability, and limits on covert tactics as mitigating measures; include reputational risk analysis as part of evaluation.
